item.title: These maps show how expensive state schools can be for low-income students
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

To avoid spending their young adult lives in debt, students have long been counseled to stay in-state for college. After all, it’s the mission of public universities, funded by tax dollars, to provide an affordable, high-quality education to state residents.

Yet, in 34 states, it costs students from low-income families at least a third of their household income — upwards of $10,000 a year — to attend the state flagship university. That includes not just tuition, but also room and board and books, after accounting for all grants and scholarships — what’s known as “net price.”

Take Alabama, which had one of the highest price tags for public colleges in the country in 2024, the most recent data available. A student coming from a family in that state that earns less than $30,000 a year was expected to pay more than $19,000 annually on average for tuition and other costs at the University of Alabama, the flagship. The same went for Pennsylvania State University.

And it’s not just flagship universities. At more than half of four-year public colleges across the country, including regional public institutions as well as large research universities, in-state students from families making less than $30,000 faced this same, near-impossible financial juggling act: On average, they had to pay more than a third of their family income to attend.

Net price at public colleges has declined over the past few years, when adjusted to overall inflation, yet wages have not kept up as the costs of housing, food and health care keep rising, and low-income families continue to struggle to afford college.

Some states have done a better job of controlling costs than others. Florida — just across the state line from Alabama — had among the least expensive four-year public colleges in the country. That’s largely because the state legislature has maintained funding for higher education and capped tuition over the past decade.

Hover over the map to see the cost for each state.

Even if students from families earning less than $30,000 take out the maximum federal student loan allowed ($5,500 for first-year students), attending one of nearly 300 public four-year colleges still cost them at least $4,500 more in their first year alone, even when they stayed in-state. The same was true at more than 50 public two-year colleges that also offer bachelor’s degrees.

Hover over each dot to see the name of the college and the average cost.

The situation wasn’t much better for students from families making between $30,000 and $48,000. They needed to come up with a sizable share of their annual income, $5,000 — after all scholarships and maximum student loans — at close to 300 four-year public colleges, even when they enrolled in-state.

About 1 in 6 American households earns less than $30,000 a year. More than 1 in 4 earn less than $50,000.

State flagship universities boast some of the highest graduation and job placement rates among public universities, which makes them a crucial path to a secure financial future for students who grew up in poverty. Their affordability, however, depends on where you live.

Students from families who make less than $30,000 paid just over $1,000 out of pocket for tuition and other costs at the University of Michigan and roughly $2,000 at the state flagships in Florida, North Carolina and Illinois. Pennsylvania State University and the University of Alabama were the most expensive for low-income families, but the state flagships in New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon and Iowa all also cost students whose families make less than $30,000 more than half their annual income.

It’s not just the flagship that’s pricey in Alabama. The state’s other public colleges were among the most expensive in the country on average for families who make less than $48,000. (A spokesman from the University of Alabama said that the average net price for families making less than $30,000 dropped by about 6 percent in 2024-25, which brought it to about $18,000; it decreased by 12 percent for families making between $30,001 and $48,000, he said.)

The University of North Alabama, which cost low-income students the least in the state, still had a net price of close to $10,000. And half of Alabama’s public colleges cost more than $14,000 for students whose families make less than $30,000.

There are less expensive public colleges scattered around the country, and some students save money by starting at a community college and then transferring, although that path isn’t always available. At just over 60 public four-year colleges, the net price for families who make less than $30,000 was $5,000 or less in 2024. New York City, where most students don’t live on campus, hosts seven colleges that cost less than $1,600.

Methodology:

Where does this data come from? These charts use the federal government’s definition of net price, which is an attempt to capture the total cost of attendance for a student. It includes room and board, books and supplies, tuition and required fees, minus any grants and scholarships for first-time, full-time, dependent students (those who are still under the care of their parents). We use the income brackets of below $30,000 and between $30,000 and $48,000, because that’s how the data is kept in the Integrated Post-Secondary Data System (IPEDS). Median household income nationally was about $81,600 in 2024, but it varies widely by state, from a high of close to $105,000 in Massachusetts to about $59,000 in Mississippi.

How did we choose which dataset to use?…

item.title: What Schools Still Don’t Teach About Interest Rates and Why It Matters
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Most people leave school able to calculate interest on paper. Far fewer leave knowing what interest will do to their lives. That gap is easy to miss because it doesn’t show up on a report card. It shows up years later, in loan papers, credit card statements and savings balances that never seem to grow.

The problem isn’t that schools ignore math. Interest is taught as a formula, and the formula stops at the edge of the worksheet. Students learn how to find an answer but not how to read the numbers that will shape what they borrow, what they save and what they can afford. To close that gap, it helps to look at what gets left out, starting with how the subject is framed in the first place.

The Gap Between Arithmetic and Everyday Money

Formulas Without Consequences

A typical lesson on interest gives students a principal, a rate and a time period, then asks them to solve for the total. It’s tidy and it can be graded. It also hides almost everything that matters. Real rates change. Real balances get added to and drawn down. Real people make choices partway through, and those choices change the outcome.

When interest only ever appears as a problem with one right answer, students learn to treat it as a puzzle rather than as a force acting on their money every day.

Interest Is a Price

The simplest idea missing from many classrooms is also the most useful one. Interest is the price of money over time. When you borrow, you pay that price. When you save, someone pays it to you. Once students see interest as a price, they start asking the questions they would ask about any purchase. Is this a good deal? Can I find it cheaper somewhere else? What happens if I wait?

That shift in thinking matters most when you see how interest builds over long stretches of time.

How Compounding Actually Feels Over Time

The Slow Start That Fools People

Compounding means you earn interest on your interest. Most students can repeat that definition. What they rarely get is a feel for how lopsided the results are.

Put $1,000 in an account earning 5% a year and leave it alone. In the first year, you earn $50. Nothing to get excited about. By year 30, the balance has grown to about $4,322, and that single year alone adds more than $200. The growth was always there, but it took decades to become obvious. People who expect fast results often give up during the slow early years, which is exactly when patience pays off most.

A quick shortcut called the rule of 72 makes this easier to grasp. Divide 72 by the interest rate, and you get a rough idea of how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, that’s about 12 years. A tool like the compound interest calculator on the SEC’s Investor.gov site lets students test different rates and time frames and watch the curve bend upward.

Compounding Runs in Both Directions

The same math that rewards savers punishes borrowers. A credit card charging 24% APR works out to about 2% a month. On a $3,000 balance, that’s roughly $60 in interest in the first month. If you pay $75, only $15 actually goes toward what you owe. The balance barely moves, and the card company is happy to keep it that way.

Students who understand this early tend to treat credit cards very differently. Still, knowing how compounding works is only half the picture. The other half is knowing which rate you’re actually dealing with.

Why the Rate You See Is Rarely the Rate You Pay

APR, APY and the Fine Print

Banks and lenders use different terms for a reason. APR, or annual percentage rate, is often used for loans and doesn’t always show the effect of compounding. APY, or annual percentage yield, does. A 12% APR compounded monthly actually costs about 12.68% over a year. The gap looks small until it’s multiplied across a large balance or a long loan.

Few students are ever shown these two terms side by side. As a result, many adults compare offers without realizing they’re comparing different measurements.

Inflation Eats Quietly

Even a correct rate can mislead you if inflation is ignored. If your savings earn 1% while prices rise 3%, your balance goes up but what it can buy goes down. Economists call the difference the real return. The Consumer Price Index published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics is the standard way to track how fast prices are rising, and checking it against your savings rate is a sobering exercise.

That raises a fair question. If rates matter this much, who decides what they are?

Where Rates Come From

The Central Bank’s Role

Rates don’t appear out of nowhere. In the United States, the Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate, which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans. That rate ripples outward into mortgages, car loans, credit cards and savings accounts.

Why Your Rate Moves, or Doesn’t

Some rates follow the Fed closely. Variable credit card rates often rise within weeks of a hike. Others lag behind or barely move at all. Many large banks are slow to raise what they pay savers, even when borrowing costs climb. Knowing this helps people spot when they’re being underpaid and gives them a reason to act. The easiest place to put that knowledge to work is a savings account.

Savings Accounts as a Practical Classroom

Watching Interest Work in Real Time

A savings account turns abstract lessons into something you can see each month. Deposits go in, interest gets added and the balance changes without any effort. For a young person, watching even a few dollars of interest arrive can make compounding feel real in a way no textbook can. It also builds a habit, and habits tend to outlast lessons.

Savings accounts carry little risk, too. Deposits at insured banks are protected up to set limits, which makes them a calm place to learn how rates behave before moving on to investments that can lose value.

Shopping for a Better Rate…

item.title: 8 Tools To Measure Reading Levels Of Texts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful for educators

Lexile Level Alternatives

Reading assessment tools measure different things: how accurately a student reads, what the student understands, or how difficult a text is likely to be.

A student who reads a passage accurately may still misunderstand it. Research distinguishes word recognition from the language and knowledge needed for comprehension (Castles et al., 2018). Choose an assessment by the question it needs to answer.

Which tool fits the task?

Tools for assessing students

1. DIBELS 8th Edition

DIBELS uses short assessments to identify students who may need reading support and measure progress. Its oral reading fluency assessment, used in grades 1–8, requires a student to read a supplied passage aloud for one minute while the teacher marks errors on a separate copy.

Skipped or incorrectly read words count as errors. If a student hesitates for three seconds, the examiner supplies the word and marks it incorrect. A word self-corrected within three seconds counts as correct. The teacher calculates words correct per minute and reading accuracy, then checks the benchmark for the student’s grade and testing period.

The oral reading scores do not directly test understanding of the passage. Fuchs et al. (2001) reviewed evidence supporting oral reading fluency as an indicator of broader reading competence. That research supports the assessment approach; it does not, by itself, validate the current DIBELS edition.

Access: Download student passages, scoring forms, benchmarks, and administration instructions from the University of Oregon’s DIBELS materials page at no cost. Follow the administration guide and do not rehearse assessment passages with students.

2. easyCBM

easyCBM provides reading assessments and graphs showing a student’s scores across testing dates. Tasks include reading words or passages aloud and answering multiple-choice comprehension questions. Available measures depend on grade and account type.

A teacher can administer different passage-reading forms at successive checks and enter the scores to track words correct per minute. Use designated progress-monitoring forms at the same assessment level; changing passage difficulty makes the scores harder to compare.

Access: Create an account through easyCBM’s Teacher Edition. The free Lite tier includes progress-monitoring assessments, individual graphs, and item-level reports. Benchmark assessments and benchmark risk reports require a paid edition. The edition comparison lists which measures each account includes.

3. Qualitative Reading Inventory, Seventh Edition (QRI-7)

QRI-7 is an individually administered assessment with graded word lists and narrative and informational passages from pre-primer through high school. Teachers record oral reading errors and assess understanding through retelling and questions about the passage.

Teachers use the inventory’s criteria to estimate independent, instructional, and frustration levels for the passages assessed. These results describe performance on those tasks; they are not interchangeable with a Lexile measure.

Access: Purchase QRI-7 from Pearson or use a school-owned copy. The manual includes administration, scoring, and technical-development information. Administration requires time for one-to-one reading, comprehension questions, and scoring.

4. Star Reading

Star Reading is a computer-adaptive assessment: question difficulty changes in response to the student’s answers. Students answer questions on a device; Renaissance reports a typical testing time of about 20 minutes.

Reports include a scaled score for tracking performance and a percentile rank for comparison with students in the same grade. Schools use these results to screen students and monitor achievement.

Because Star Reading does not assess oral reading, its results do not show which words a student mispronounces or how the student reads aloud.

Access: Students and teachers sign in through their school’s Renaissance subscription. Star Reading and Star Early Literacy are separate assessments; verify which one the school provides.

Tools for checking text difficulty

5. Lexile Find a Book and Text Analyzer

Find a Book lets teachers look up a book or search by Lexile measure and interest. Use it to identify possible texts when a student already has a Lexile measure from an assessment. Searching by the student’s enrolled grade does not establish that student’s reading ability.

The classroom Text Analyzer accepts prose passages of up to 500 words and returns a 200L-wide range, rather than a single certified measure. It is not designed to produce valid measures for poetry, song lyrics, recipes, or lists.

Access: Both tools are available through the Lexile & Quantile Hub. Find a Book offers limited searches without registration and unlimited searches with a free Basic+ account. Text Analyzer requires Premium access; eligible educators in partner states receive it at no cost after registering with their school or district email address.

6. Microsoft Word readability statistics

Word reports Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level, calculated from average sentence length and syllables per word. Teachers can use these statistics to check assignment directions or compare drafts of a passage.

Access: In Word for Microsoft 365 on the Current Channel, select Home → Editor → Document stats. Other supported versions use proofing settings. Microsoft’s readability instructions give the steps by version. The feature is included with supported Word software; it does not assess a student.

Use the result to choose the next check

If a student reads slowly or makes frequent errors, examine word reading more closely. If the student reads accurately but cannot explain the passage, assess comprehension rather than assigning a lower level from speed alone. Record the tool, date, passage or test level, and score so later results can be compared meaningfully.…
